entry: Group of territories controlled by a monarch or supreme central authority, usually created by conquest. Within an empire, different populations may have different sets of rights and may be governed differently. Scholars typically distinguish empires from nation-states by the hierarchy of rights and prestige among their peoples. Territorial empires, such as the Macedonian and [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] empires, extend outward from an original frontier. A *thalassocracy* is a maritime empire of islands and coasts that requires a powerful navy, as with the Athenian-dominated [[Delian League]] and the [[British Empire]]. The word derives from the Roman concept of *imperium*, the right to command. Empires have taken many forms throughout history.

19th-century [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] in South America (1822–1889), covering modern [[Brazil]] and, until 1828, [[Uruguay]]. A colony of Portugal, Brazil became the seat of the [[Portuguese Empire]] in 1808, when the Portuguese court fled [[Napoleon]]'s invasion of Portugal and settled in [[Rio de Janeiro]]. On September 7, 1822, Prince Pedro declared independence and was acclaimed as Pedro I. He abdicated in 1831 in favor of his five-year-old son, Pedro II, whose regency was marked by regional civil wars. After Pedro II came of age, the empire achieved peace and stability and was victorious in the Platine War, the Uruguayan War and the [[Paraguayan War]]. Slavery was restricted by successive laws and abolished in 1888. A military coup on November 15, 1889, overthrew the emperor and established the First Brazilian Republic.

Japanese nation state (1868–1947), also known as Imperial Japan. It began with the [[Meiji Restoration]] on January 3, 1868, and under the slogan "Enrich the Country, Strengthen the Armed Forces" underwent large-scale industrialization and militarization. Economic turmoil in the 1920s, including the [[Great Depression]], fed militarism and nationalism, and Japan joined the [[Axis powers]] alongside Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. Its armed forces conquered much of the Asia–Pacific and committed atrocities, including the [[Nanjing Massacre]]. After the [[Attack on Pearl Harbor]] in December 1941, Japan was forced onto the defensive, and the empire surrendered on September 2, 1945. The Allied occupation under [[Douglas MacArthur]] followed, and a new constitution was enacted on May 3, 1947, ending the empire.

Early 19th-century design movement in architecture, furniture and the decorative arts, representing the second phase of [[Neoclassicism]]. It flourished between 1799 and 1815, during the Consulate and First French Empire, and was intended to idealize the rule of [[Napoleon|Napoleon I]] and the French state. Architects Charles Percier and Pierre-François-Léonard Fontaine drew on the monuments of ancient Rome and Greece. Furniture used expensive [[Mahogany|mahogany]] with gilt-bronze mounts, and buildings such as the [[Arc de Triomphe]] in [[Paris]] projected imperial power. Spreading from France across much of Europe, the style influenced the American Federal style, including the design of the [[United States Capitol]]. Both were forms of propaganda through architecture.

Epistemological view of knowledge as derived primarily from sensory experience and empirical evidence. It contrasts with [[Rationalism]], which holds that knowledge may be derived from reason independently of the senses, and with innatism, which holds that some ideas are present at birth. Empiricists argue that empirical evidence is more reliable than reasoning alone, because human reasoning is prone to cognitive biases and limitations. Historically, empiricism has been associated with the "blank slate" concept (*tabula rasa*), and its classical proponents include [[John Locke]], [[George Berkeley]] and [[David Hume]]. In the philosophy of science, empiricism underpins the scientific method: hypotheses and theories must be tested against observations of the natural world rather than resting solely on a priori reasoning, intuition or revelation.

Relationship between an employer and an employee regulating paid labor services, usually based on a [[Contract|contract]]. The employer may be a [[Corporation|corporation]], a not-for-profit organization, a co-operative or another entity. Employees are paid [[Wage|wages]] by the hour, by piecework or by annual salary, depending on the type of work, sector conditions and the parties' bargaining power. Some receive bonuses, stock options or benefits such as health insurance, housing and disability insurance. Some states require employers to contribute to social security and [[Pension|pension]] schemes. Classification is often disputed: an independent contractor controls how work is done, serves the public at large and provides their own tools, whereas an employee is paid regularly, works set hours and is closely monitored. In the [[United States]], workers are presumed to be employees unless specific guidelines are met, and a company commissioning work from a contractor does not own the [[Copyright|copyright]] unless it secures a written work-for-hire contract or a copyright assignment.

Manchu noblewoman and regent of the late [[Qing dynasty]], 1861–1908. A concubine of the Xianfeng Emperor, she bore the son who became the Tongzhi Emperor. After the Xianfeng Emperor's death in 1861 she shared the regency with Empress Dowager Ci'an, and later installed her nephew as the Guangxu Emperor. Cixi rejected Western political institutions but supported technological and military modernization. In 1898 she suppressed the Hundred Days' Reform and placed the Guangxu Emperor under house arrest; he probably died of arsenic poisoning, though no reliable source establishes who was responsible. During the [[Boxer Rebellion]] she initially backed the Boxers and declared war on foreign powers, then fled to [[Xi'an]] when the Eight-Nation Alliance occupied [[Beijing]]. Her later reforms aimed at a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]]. Her legacy is contested. She was widely portrayed as a ruthless reactionary, but some revisionist historians argue she was scapegoated for structural problems and credit her with pragmatic reform and support for [[Peking University]].

Bavarian-born Habsburg consort, Empress of Austria and Queen of Hungary by marriage to [[Franz Joseph I]]. Known as Sisi, she found the formal Habsburg court suffocating and developed a deep bond with Hungary, helping to bring about the dual monarchy of [[Austria-Hungary]] in 1867. Her son, Crown Prince Rudolf, died with his mistress in a murder–suicide at Mayerling in 1889, a blow from which she never fully recovered, and she traveled widely thereafter. She was stabbed to death in [[Geneva]] by an Italian anarchist. Her tenure of 44 years was the longest of any Austrian empress.

Unique mathematical set containing no elements, with [[Cardinality|cardinality]] zero. Its existence is either an [[Axiom|axiom]] of some set theories or can be deduced in others, and by the principle of extensionality there is only one such set. The symbol ∅ was introduced by the Bourbaki group in 1939. The empty set is a [[Subset|subset]] of every set, the [[Union (set theory)|union]] of any set with it is that set, and its [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] with any set is empty. Because zero is the identity element for addition, the sum of the elements of the empty set is taken to be zero, and by the same logic its product is one. Some texts call it the "null set", a term that in measure theory denotes a set of measure zero that need not be empty.

Large flightless bird (*Dromaius novaehollandiae*) endemic to [[Australia]]. It is the tallest native bird there and the only living member of its genus, and it is the third-tallest living bird after the [[Common ostrich|common ostrich]] and the Somali ostrich. Adults can reach 1.9 m (6 ft 3 in) and sprint at 48 km/h (30 mph). Emus are omnivorous and can go for weeks without eating. Breeding takes place in May and June; the male incubates the eggs, which hatch after about eight weeks, and fathers raise the young. Rated least concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, emus are nonetheless endangered in some local populations, and the insular subspecies became extinct after the European settlement of Australia in 1788. The emu appears on the coat of arms and on various coins, and it features in Indigenous Australian mythologies.

[[Mixture|Mixture]] of two or more normally immiscible liquids, one dispersed as droplets in the other. Emulsions are a type of [[Colloid|colloid]], and the term narrowly refers to systems in which both phases are liquids. Oil and water can form an oil-in-water emulsion, in which oil is dispersed in water, or a water-in-oil emulsion; examples include vinaigrettes, homogenized [[Milk|milk]] and some cutting fluids. Emulsification uses an emulsifier, such as lecithin, to disperse one liquid in another. Because the many phase interfaces scatter light, emulsions look cloudy and appear white when all wavelengths are scattered equally. Microemulsions and nanoemulsions, with droplets below 100 nm, appear translucent. The term also denotes the light-sensitive layer of [[Photographic film|photographic film]], which consists of silver halide particles dispersed in [[Gelatin|gelatin]].

Icy moon of [[Saturn]], the sixth-largest moon of its planet and about 500 km in diameter. Its surface is covered by fresh snow, making it one of the most reflective bodies in the [[Solar System]]; noon temperatures reach only −198 °C. William Herschel discovered it on August 28, 1789. Little was learned until [[Voyager 1]] and [[Voyager 2]] flew past in 1980 and 1981, and the Cassini spacecraft began close flybys in 2005. Cassini found water-rich plumes erupting from the south polar region, with more than 100 geysers identified. The plumes supply most of Saturn's E ring and carry [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]] crystals and ice particles. In 2014, NASA reported evidence for a large south polar subsurface ocean of liquid water, about 10 km thick. Research suggests that its hydrothermal environment could be habitable to microorganisms similar to some on Earth, and that [[Methane|methane]] in the plumes could be produced by such organisms.

Inflammation of the brain, with symptoms including reduced or altered consciousness, [[Aphasia|aphasia]], headache, fever, confusion and a stiff neck. Complications may include seizures, hallucinations, memory problems and hearing difficulties. Causes include viruses such as [[Herpes|herpes simplex]] and [[Rabies]], bacteria, fungi and parasites, as well as [[Autoimmune disease|autoimmune diseases]] and certain medications. In 30–40% of cases the cause remains unknown. Diagnosis is based on symptoms, supported by blood tests, [[Medical imaging|medical imaging]] and analysis of cerebrospinal fluid. Some types are preventable with [[Vaccine|vaccines]]. Treatment, usually in hospital, may include antiviral drugs such as acyclovir, anticonvulsants and corticosteroids, and some patients require artificial respiration. In 2015, encephalitis was estimated to have affected 4.3 million people and caused 150,000 deaths worldwide.

In England, appropriation of common land, ending commoners' traditional rights of access and use. Enclosure took three forms: owners creating closes from common fields, groups of proprietors (usually small farmers or squires) enclosing whole parishes, and enclosure by acts of Parliament. Its stated justification was to improve agricultural efficiency, though there were other motives, such as raising the value of the land. Historians regard enclosure riots as "the pre-eminent form" of social protest from the 1530s to 1640s. After the [[Black Death]] in the middle of the 14th century, population fell and surviving laborers' wages rose, translating into [[Inflation|inflation]]. Some historians see the resulting labor shortage as contributing to the abandonment of land and the decline of the feudal system, while others argue that the plague only sped up an existing process. Parts of south-east England, notably sections of [[Essex]] and [[Kent]], retained small enclosed fields, while the open-field system lay in a broad band from [[Yorkshire]] and Lincolnshire diagonally across England.

Cryptographic process converting plaintext into ciphertext, decodable only by authorized parties. Encryption does not itself prevent interference but denies intelligible content to an interceptor. Modern schemes usually rely on a pseudo-random key generated by an algorithm; with a well-designed scheme, decryption without the key should be computationally infeasible. Early forms were used in military messaging, including the [[Caesar cipher|Caesar cipher]], which shifted each letter a fixed number of positions. By c. 800, the Arab mathematician [[Al-Kindi|al-Kindi]] had developed frequency analysis to break such ciphers. Around c. 1790, [[Thomas Jefferson]] theorized a wheel cipher for military correspondence that was never built. In [[World War II]], Germany used the [[Enigma machine]] for military communications. Modern systems use public-key and symmetric-key methods, such as [[Transport Layer Security]], which protects communication over the [[Internet]].

General-knowledge English-language encyclopedia, first published in Edinburgh in 1768–71. Its second edition ran to 10 volumes, and by the fourth edition (1801–1810) it had grown to 20. Its size, measured in total word count, has remained roughly steady at about 40 million words since the early 20th century. The 9th and 11th editions are considered landmarks of scholarship and literary style. After an American firm acquired it in 1901, the 11th edition shortened and simplified articles to appeal to North American readers. In 1932 the publisher adopted "continuous revision", reprinting each article on a schedule. The 15th edition (1974), of 32 volumes and 32,640 pages, was the last printed edition; the *Britannica* has been published online since 2016. Competitors included [[Microsoft]] Encarta and online collaborative encyclopedias, and in March 2012 the company announced it would stop printing.

General encyclopedia published in France from 1751 to 1772, central to the Enlightenment. Edited by [[Denis Diderot]] and, until 1759, by [[Jean Le Rond d'Alembert]], it drew on many contributors known as the *Encyclopédistes*. It was originally conceived as a French translation of Ephraim Chambers's *Cyclopaedia* (1728). Diderot wanted it "to change the way people think", but the first edition's price of 980 livres kept it from much of the middle class. It was the first encyclopedia to name many contributors and the first general encyclopedia to describe the mechanical arts in detail. The first edition comprised seventeen folio volumes of text and eleven volumes of engravings.

Reference work summarizing knowledge, general or specialized, usually arranged in articles. Unlike a [[Dictionary|dictionary]], which focuses on linguistic information about words, an encyclopedia article gives factual information about its subject in greater depth than a definition. Encyclopedias have existed for around 2,000 years, and their form has evolved with language, size, intent, authorship and technology. The modern encyclopedia developed from the dictionary in the 18th century. The word derives from the Greek *enkyklios paideia*, meaning "general education", but copyists of a 1470 Latin edition of Quintilian merged the phrase into a single word. Its spelling varies, with encyclopedia in American English and encyclopedia in British English, following [[Noah Webster]]'s spelling reform. Digital and open-source versions in the 21st century have greatly expanded the accessibility, authorship and readership of entries.

Language at risk of disappearing through loss or shift of its speakers. A language with no fluent speakers left is considered extinct, though a [[Language death|dead]] language may still be studied through recordings or writings. Language shift usually occurs when speakers adopt a language of greater social, economic or wider use, a process accelerated by [[Globalization|globalization]], mass migration, linguistic imperialism and neocolonialism. Between 6,000 and 7,000 languages are spoken today, and some linguists estimate that 50–90% of them will be severely endangered or dead by 2100. Most languages are spoken by fewer than 10,000 people. Revitalization projects, education and literacy programs in minority languages, and documentation of little-known languages aim to slow the loss. Regional [[Dialect|dialects]] of widely spoken languages, such as varieties of English on the American east coast, are also becoming endangered.

Species with a very high risk of extinction in the near future, worldwide or in a particular region. Species usually become endangered through [[Habitat|habitat]] loss and loss of genetic variation. Habitat is lost through agricultural, housing and industrial development, and through [[Climate change|climate change]] and [[Invasive species|invasive species]]. Reduced populations lose genetic diversity through [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]], disease and monoculture. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List classifies global status in nine groups. Criteria include a population decline of 50% to 70% over 10 years or three generations, and a population of fewer than 2,500 mature individuals after a 20% decline within five years. In 2026, the IUCN Red List named 49,500 species as threatened with extinction. Many nations protect such species by forbidding hunting, restricting land development or creating protected areas, and some are supported by captive breeding and habitat restoration.

Order of the bytes within a computer word, as stored in memory or transmitted over a communication medium. The two principal forms are big-endian, which stores the most significant byte at the lowest address, and little-endian, which stores the least significant byte first. Big-endian is the dominant order in networking protocols such as the [[Internet protocol suite]], while little-endian dominates processors such as [[X86|x86]]. Danny Cohen coined the terms in 1980, borrowing them from the debate over breaking boiled eggs in *Gulliver's Travels* by Jonathan Swift.

Hormone-producing glands releasing their products directly into the [[Circulatory system|circulatory system]]. The endocrine system is a messenger system of hormone feedback loops that regulate distant organs. In humans the major endocrine glands are the [[Thyroid|thyroid]], parathyroid, [[Pituitary gland|pituitary]], pineal and adrenal glands, and the testes or ovaries; the hypothalamus, [[Pancreas|pancreas]] and thymus also have endocrine functions. The thyroid secretes thyroxine, the pituitary growth hormone, the pineal melatonin and the testes [[Testosterone|testosterone]]. The hypothalamus, the neural control center for endocrine systems in vertebrates, links the endocrine system to the [[Nervous system|nervous system]] via the pituitary. Unlike exocrine glands, which have ducts, endocrine glands are ductless and highly vascular. The study of the system and its disorders is endocrinology, a branch of internal medicine.

Disease marked by growth of uterine-lining tissue outside the [[Uterus|uterus]], most often on the ovaries, fallopian tubes or pelvic lining. It can also appear on the bowel, bladder, lungs or skin. It affects about 10% of women of reproductive age. Symptoms include pelvic pain, heavy and painful periods, painful intercourse and [[Infertility|infertility]], and they tend to ease after [[Menopause|menopause]]. Diagnosis commonly takes 5–12 years. Treatment usually combines hormonal treatment with an anti-inflammatory drug such as [[Naproxen|naproxen]]; surgery may remove lesions, but in a substantial minority of cases the disease returns. There is no cure.

Membrane-enclosed organelle of eukaryotic cells, forming a network of sacs and tubules that processes [[Protein|proteins]]. The rough ER (RER) is studded with [[Ribosome|ribosomes]], the sites of protein synthesis, and is especially prominent in [[Liver|liver]] cells. The smooth ER (SER) lacks ribosomes and carries out lipid synthesis, production of [[Steroid|steroid]] hormones and detoxification. The ER is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane and is absent from red blood cells and [[Sperm|sperm]]. Charles Garnier observed it by light microscopy in 1897, coining the term ergastoplasm, and its lacy membranes were first seen by electron microscopy in 1945.

Closed drainage basin retaining its water, with no outflow to rivers or oceans. Water flows instead into permanent and seasonal lakes and swamps that reach balance through [[Evaporation|evaporation]]. Such basins are also called terminal, closed or internal drainage systems. They are most common in [[Desert|desert]] regions, where low rainfall or rapid evaporation concentrates dissolved minerals, making many lakes saline. Endorheic basins constitute local base levels for erosion and deposition. Endorheic water bodies include the [[Caspian Sea]], the world's largest inland body of water.
